newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico drug lord mourned at his home.
newsitem.headline: Mexico drug lord mourned at his home.

text.p: Inside the home of the man considered Mexico's most wanted drug lord were all the trappings of death: a grieving mother, floral wreaths, carloads of mourners. The only thing missing was the corpse.

The family of Amado Carrillo Fuentes said on Saturday that he died in a Mexico City hospital on Friday while undergoing plastic surgery under a false name. Mexican authorities said after conducting fingerprint tests the alleged trafficker's death was "probable" but they needed further tests to be sure.

Before the death was made public, the Carrillo family had the corpse flown quietly from the capital to a funeral parlour in their home state of Sinaloa, apparently hoping to give the billionaire fugitive a stylish and discreet burial.

But no sooner had Carrillo's 63-year-old mother, Aurora Fuentes de Carrillo, identified the corpse on Saturday night than scores of submachinegun-toting police bore down on the San Martin funeral home and snatched the body in its metallic gray coffin.
Plainclothes detectives, automatic rifles at the ready, shut down the airport in the city of Culiacan as the coffin was flown under cover of darkness back to Mexico City.

Sitting stiffly at her carefully tended ranch at 3 a.m. on Sunday, a black-clad Dona Aurora, as Carrillo's mother is deferentially known for miles around this farming community, fumed over what she considered an unpardonable outrage.
"The treated us terribly badly. They beat us and they threatened to kill us," she told a handful of reporters admitted into the heavily guarded ranch.

Surrounded by Louis XV-style furniture and mounds of gold-rimmed china and crystal, she told of her grief. An artist's portrait of a youthful Amado Carrillo stood in a corner, almost hidden by floral tributes.
"I want him here in my house. We want to bury him. I can understand, I suppose, that if he were alive they would take him away. But a lifeless corpse, why do they want it?"

As servants bustled around with walkie-talkies, arranging 8-foot (2.2-metre) wreaths, Fuentes insisted the corpse was that of her son, who was believed to be 42 when he died. She said police who seized the body told her she would have to travel to Mexico City, 620 miles (1,000 km) away, to get it back.
Mexico's Attorney-General's Office said it was awaiting final test results on the body although initial tests gave "indications" that the corpse was that of Carrillo.

Carrillo's friends, some driving new four-wheel-drive vehicles with dark windows, others dressed as farmworkers, turned up at the ranch through the night to offer condolences. Some mourners in black clothes, snakeskin boots and Texan cowboy hats shouted to reporters to tell the truth about the man his mother called a model son.

Mexican and U.S. officials had accused Carrillo of flying billions of dollars' worth of Colombian cocaine to the United States via Mexico. He was the subject of at least 26 investigations by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.
But Fuentes denied Cabrillo was the notorious "Lord of the Skies." She normally describes her son as a farmer.
Natalia Lopez, an old family employee standing at Fuentes' side, remembered a little boy she "used to take to the tomato fields," adding: "He was working as soon as he could walk."
The ranch itself has grown from a small holding worked from horseback when Carrillo was born into a beacon of prosperity, with manicured lawns and its own chapel.
